summary: ORBITA is a bilingual browser-based space mission simulation game that allows 1–4 players to experience the complete process of designing, managing, and operating a space mission. Players begin by defining a scientific objective, then make strategic decisions about spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, orbital trajectories, and ground communication networks. The game features an interconnected resource management system covering six critical resources, where every decision creates a chain of consequences that affects overall mission performance. During the flight simulation, players must respond to unexpected mission anomalies and adapt their strategies to keep the mission on track. One of ORBITA’s most innovative features is its Tradespace Visualization System, which compares the player's design with 240 alternative mission configurations, demonstrating that there is no single perfect solution and that every design involves trade-offs between cost, performance, and available resources. By combining scientific principles, NASA-related data, interactive simulations, and collaborative decision-making, ORBITA makes complex space engineering more accessible and engaging. More importantly, it helps players develop critical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, and resource management skills while understanding the challenges of real-world space exploration.
details:
What it does and how it works

ORBITA is a bilingual (English/Vietnamese) browser game in which 1–4 players design, launch and operate a complete space mission. Players choose one of four scenarios: a Mekong Delta flood-watch satellite, a lunar south-pole ice orbiter, a Mars water orbiter, or a space telescope searching for life. Following NASA's four mission segments (User, Space, Launch, Ground) and JPL's Concept Maturity Levels 1–4, they set science objectives first. They then drag instruments, solar arrays, batteries, antennas and engines onto their spacecraft, and pick an orbit, a launch vehicle, a constellation size, a lifetime and a ground network. A live engine recalculates six resources after every choice: mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. A design review modeled on NASA Goddard's Mission Design Lab explains every problem in plain language. Players then fly the launch themselves (easing off through Max-Q, staging on time, cutting off at orbital speed) and time the orbit-insertion burn. In mission control they respond to random anomalies such as solar storms, debris, wheel failures, budget cuts, Mars dust storms and a real-time Mekong flood alert. A post-mission report scores mission performance, science value, resource efficiency, decision quality and teamwork. It explains why the mission succeeded or failed and compares the design with real NASA missions such as NISAR, LRO, MRO and Webb.

Benefits

Students rarely get to experience a whole mission from idea to operations. ORBITA makes engineering trade-offs visible and hands-on instead of theoretical. Every click shows a "consequence chain" (heavier → more propellant → bigger rocket). Players can redesign and fly again as many times as they like, so they learn from both success and failure. It is free, needs no install or account, runs on phones and low-cost computers, and works in Vietnamese and English.

Expected impact

ORBITA is built for middle-school to university students, teachers and STEM clubs, especially in Vietnam and other countries where space engineering courses are rare. The Mekong Delta scenario links satellite design to a real problem affecting millions of people. The User segment teaches that space data creates value only when it reaches farmers, rescuers and communities. Team mode turns a classroom into a mission team with real roles, which builds collaboration and communication skills. Shareable design codes and a leaderboard let classes compare solutions and compete.

Tools and technologies

HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript in a single file with no frameworks, so it loads fast on any device. Graphics use SVG and the Canvas API (spacecraft drawing, flyable launch, orbit animation, charts). Sound uses the Web Audio API, drag-and-drop uses Pointer Events, and progress is saved in local storage. The leaderboard uses the Claude Artifacts database. The physics models are simplified from NASA resources: the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Δv per orbit, solar power by distance from the Sun, eclipse-based battery sizing, data rates falling with distance, the Deep Space Network, and reliability per year. Testing was done with Playwright on phone and desktop screen sizes. The code and texts were drafted with an AI assistant (Claude) under the team's direction, and the team reviewed the science and tested the game.

Creativity

1. Learning by doing: players assemble the spacecraft by drag-and-drop and personally pilot the launch and the orbit burn, so their skill affects the outcome.

2. A consequence chain after every decision.

3. A tradespace map that automatically closes 240 alternative designs and plots them with the Pareto frontier, the way NASA design labs explore options. It shows that there is no single perfect solution and tells players whether a cheaper or better design exists.

4. Team play for up to four people on one device with roles (Mission Lead & Science, Spacecraft Engineer, Orbit & Launch, Comms & Ground). Every role must sign off before launch, and each anomaly is routed to the right person.

5. A mission patch generated from each player's design and result.

Factors the team considered

Scientific validity with simple, transparent formulas shown inside the game; accessibility for different skill levels (three difficulties, hints, a mentor character, a sandbox); local relevance (Mekong floods, Vietnamese language); mobile-first design for students without computers; clear feedback on why a mission succeeds or fails; replayability; fair scoring that rewards good decisions, not just big budgets; collaboration; and using all nine NASA and partner resources from the challenge page. NASA does not endorse this project.
